01 / The whole system

How your
backtest works.

The program uses saved company data and prices to select stocks. It then checks how those stocks performed.

This guide explains each part, how the parts connect, and why some runs take longer. You do not need to read the code.

Saved dataOne set of selection rulesFour ways to use itNo downloads during a backtest

The main data flow

Save once. Prepare once.
Select many times.

A cache is saved data that the program can use again. Select a step to see its job.

1. The source data stays on your computer.

The raw folder holds the saved inputs. Ordinary preparation and backtests read these files. They do not contact the data supplier.

The browser and Python use the same selection rules. They use different prepared records for different dates.

02 / Four ways to use it

The date choice sets the path.

Latest picks and January backtests work in the saved HTML page. Custom dates and random dates need the local Python service.

Prepared in advance · Runs in the browser

A saved January-to-January test.

Prepared January records→Data inside the HTML→Browser selection→Results

The program buys stocks each January. It sells them at the next January date. The last book can cover part of a year.

Change the group, filters, metric or stock count in the browser. The page uses records already inside the HTML. It does not prepare new daily books.

Prepared in advance · Runs in the browser

A screen for the latest saved session.

Prepared latest records→Data inside the HTML→Browser selection→Stock list

Latest means the latest SPY session in the saved data. It does not mean a live market feed.

A company needs a price on that exact session. The saved company list must mark it as listed. Old stopped prices are excluded. These picks have no future holding return.

Prepared when needed · Uses the local Python service

A test on your chosen calendar.

Browser request→Local Python service→Saved or new dated books→Results in the browser

Choose the start date, end date and rebalance interval. Supported intervals are 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 months.

Trade dates move forward to a saved SPY session. The end mark moves back to a session. A new buy/sell date pair usually needs a new book. A saved pair can be reused.

Many dated tests · Uses the local Python service

The same strategy on different trade dates.

Sample trade dates→Plan shared missing books→Calculate books in parallel→Save complete trials in order→Compare trial results

For each trial, the program selects one trading session from each frequency block. The last partial block also participates. Actual holding periods can have different lengths.

Trials use the same start and end window. Strategy and SPY hold cash until the first trade. The program plans shared date pairs once. Separate worker processes calculate missing books ahead. One writer saves complete trials in order.

New runs use fresh dates by default. A seed is a number that lets you repeat the date choices. Use the same saved settings and seed to replay a batch.

What happens when you double-click start.cmd?

Run backtest-web.cmd in Windows Terminal, or double-click start.cmd. The website stays attached to this terminal on 0.0.0.0:3000. Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 on this computer. The terminal shows server logs. Press Ctrl+C to stop. A new launch stops this project’s identified server and starts current code in the new terminal. This also replaces an older background instance. A startup lock serializes preparation and binding. A lifetime lock stays held until the listener and all request threads close. A stopped HTTP endpoint does not release ownership. A replacement waits up to 30 seconds, then asks you to wait or stop the old terminal and retry. Python prepares stale caches and builds before it opens the browser. An unrelated port owner is left running; the website uses a free port.

Development and runtime

Edit in WSL.
Run native Windows code.

The WSL source checkout owns code and Git history. The Windows runtime owns saved market data, prepared databases, logs and local builds.

WSL source→Committed source deployment→Windows runtime

From WSL, run python3 tools/deploy.py --start. From Windows Terminal, run the installed backtest-web.cmd. The current WSL deployment tool retains the installed commit before starting native Windows Python in that terminal. Experimental commits do not change this default. The source checkout is . The runtime is . The original legacy folder remains a fallback.

What does deployment change?

Deployment publishes one Git commit. Normal publication selects the installed commit from data/deployment.json. A fresh runtime requires an explicit revision. Use python3 tools/deploy.py --revision <commit> --start from WSL to deliberately select another revision. An explicit --revision HEAD requests a change. It does not qualify an experimental engine. Working-tree edits stay in WSL. The runtime has no separate Git repository. Source file hashes and the deployed commit are recorded in data/deployment.json. Only source files owned by the preceding deployment can be removed. Unexpected source edits or conflicting local files stop publication.

Raw data, databases, environments, logs, the local website build and baseline revision history stay on Windows. The current verified report also stays there. Source deployment does not overwrite that report. Use python3 tools/deploy.py --collect-report to collect a database-bound report revision and priced evidence for review and source commit.

How are running servers protected?

The entry point website/serve.py takes shared source ownership before importing website/serve_app.py. It holds ownership through server cleanup. website/runtime_access.py owns this boundary. Deployment stops authenticated instances from this runtime, including alternate ports. It waits for process exit, then takes exclusive source ownership and financial cache ownership. Unknown listeners remain running.

An interrupted source publication leaves data/deployment.pending.json. Startup refuses to import the application while that journal exists. Run deployment again to finish the verified publication. Default retry selects the journal’s commit. It does not restore the older manifest commit after recovery. An explicit different revision is rejected before staging. Finish recovery before selecting another revision. Do not remove the journal to bypass recovery.

The wave8 revision safeguard is in WSL source. The running website stays on its installed engine. Its launcher already delegates normal starts to the current WSL tool. The updated forwarding of explicit revision arguments is source-only until installed. Use the WSL command above for explicit selection with the older installed launcher. No live restart or deployment was used to verify this safeguard.

Where do tests run?

WSL runs source and synthetic checks. python3 tools/deploy.py --check deploys committed code and runs the installed Windows checks, including saved-data path checks, preparation and browser parity. It does not download market data. Each operating system has its own environment and compiled caches.

03 / One holding period

From a report to a portfolio.

A book describes one buy date and one sell or mark date. The dated engine prepares the requested stock group before it applies your final filters.

  1. Choose a usable annual report.

    The report becomes available 90 days after its year-end. Availability must be before the buy date. A report older than 800 days is excluded.

  2. Prepare the requested stock group.

    The original group keeps the original 250-name screen. The broader group uses companies with saved prices. Only the requested group is prepared. Neither group covers the full market.

  3. Estimate values at the buy date.

    The program uses saved prices to update report market cap. It adds report net debt to estimate enterprise value. A missing buy price excludes a stock.

  4. Prepare metrics and holding returns.

    The program calculates both supported EBITDA metrics for the requested group. It uses dividend-adjusted prices for holding returns. It saves these records for the date pair.

  5. Filter, rank, then select.

    The program reads your chosen group. It applies your filters before ranking. Lower selected EV/EBITDA multiples rank first. It takes the ranks you request.

  6. Calculate the portfolio result.

    Each selected stock starts with the same weight. The program averages their holding returns. It joins the periods and compares the result with SPY.

Period return = sum of selected stock returns ÷ actual selected stock count
What if a stock stops trading?

The historical engine uses its last available price. The proceeds stay as cash until the next rebalance. A listed bankruptcy override gives a total loss. The override list is currently empty.

A later delisting does not change an earlier sale price. The original review covered 37 early stops. Additional stops in expanded or dated tests have not all received that review.

What if too few stocks pass the screen?

The program uses the stocks that pass. If 80 stocks pass a top-100 request, each starts with a weight of 1/80.

An empty holding period makes full-window strategy growth and CAGR unavailable. Random-date summaries keep incomplete trials visible. They exclude these trials from both paired distributions.

Which financial values are used?

The original saved annual record includes market cap, enterprise value and EV/EBITDA. Additional annual statement assets supply the financial ratio filters. The program derives EBITDA and net debt from those values.

Estimated EV equals estimated market cap plus report net debt. The three-year metric uses mean EBITDA from three consecutive annual reports. Missing years exclude the stock from that metric.

The 90-day delay is an availability assumption. It is not proof of the actual filing date. Supplier data can include later revisions.

04 / Groups, filters and counts

Three choices. Three different jobs.

The stock group sets where to look. Filters set which stocks can pass. The stock count sets how many to take.

The stock group / Pool

Where should the program look?

Original candidate set: the original 250-name screen, with its report-size rules. Missing prices can reduce the usable count.

All stocks with cached prices: a broader saved-price group. It is still a partial market universe.

Filters and stock count

Which stocks, and how many?

Filters: market-cap bounds, minimum EV, selected metric yield, maximum multiple, sector and exchange. Add multiple conditions with a metric, less than or more than, and a value. All conditions must pass before ranking. Use two conditions on one metric to set a range.

Count: top 50, top 100, or a rank range. Top 100 does not expand the original 250-name screen.

Explore a setting change · Explanation only

Use the original candidate set. Apply your filters, rank the matching stocks, then take up to 50 stocks. Saved books for the same dates can be reused.

Combine conditions before ranking.

Available conditions include market cap, enterprise value, both EV/EBITDA multiples, EBITDA/EV yield, and trailing 1-year and 3-year returns. Values use the units in each label: millions of dollars, percent, or multiples. Comparisons are strict. An equal value does not pass.

Trailing returns use dividend-adjusted closes on or before the screen date and its calendar anniversary. Each endpoint must be within seven calendar days. A leap-day anniversary clamps to 28 February. No future holding return is used. A missing value fails only a condition that needs it. Latest, January, custom and random views share these rules.

The saved books include these filter values. Changing conditions reuses the books. Source or input changes require offline preparation and a website rebuild. Reload an open page to use the new build.

Financial ratios use annual statement inputs.

Download Full annual financial data in Manage backtest data. This saves full provider responses for annual income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements, key metrics and ratios for the chosen stock group. Every returned field is kept, including nulls, other currencies and filing metadata. Calculations select eligible USD inputs separately. The raw cache keeps fields for future metric calculations. Multiple records can have the same fiscal date. The raw cache keeps every returned row. For each numerical input, matching values can be used. Conflicting values stay unavailable. Response order does not select a revision. Then rebuild and reload the strategy page. Missing inputs exclude a stock only when a condition needs them.

P/E is screen-date market cap divided by annual net income. P/B uses annual stockholders’ equity. Free cash flow is shown in millions of USD. Its yield is free cash flow divided by screen-date market cap, in percent. Price/free cash flow uses the inverse ratio. Net profit margin is net income divided by revenue, in percent.

ROE uses net income divided by average stockholders’ equity from the selected and previous fiscal years, in percent. Both equity values must be positive. Current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Interest coverage is EBIT divided by interest expense. Debt/equity is total debt divided by stockholders’ equity.

PEG is screen-date P/E divided by three-year diluted EPS compound annual growth, in percentage points. It needs positive diluted EPS in four consecutive fiscal years and positive growth. No analyst forecasts are used. Ratio denominators must be positive. Missing or invalid ratios stay absent. Negative cash flow and profit margins remain valid filter values.

All annual inputs match the selected report date. The same 90-day lag, strict availability rule and 800-day age limit apply. A newer report cannot fill missing fields in an older report. Supplier revisions and EPS split treatment can affect results. The existing EBITDA-based stock groups remain the starting universe.

The controls above explain the architecture. They do not select real stocks or run a backtest.

05 / What gets reused

A new setting is not always a new book.

The dated engine saves each buy/sell date pair. It tracks completed stock groups separately. Your final filters and ranks use that group’s prepared records.

How do I check or download missing data?

Open Manage backtest data from the strategy page. Choose the stock group, symbols and price date range. Check the saved universe, annual financials, stock prices, SPY prices and Treasury yields. Export the check report if needed.

Check saved files→Download missing data→Rebuild prepared data→Open strategy page

A check does not download data or read the API key. Downloads require a button press and use the local FMP key file. The page receives only a key-file presence flag. Raw records already saved are kept. One cache reader validates annual records for both preparation and group inspection. Valid annual rows survive repair of a damaged record. The original financial downloader fills missing symbols. The full-data downloader fills missing endpoint assets for the chosen group. Older trimmed key metrics can be backfilled separately without rewriting baseline inputs. New key-metric downloads also retain every returned field. The price downloader fills ranges outside each saved date span. It does not refresh existing reports or company profiles.

The downloader uses up to 32 parallel requests. It reuses HTTP connections. Compressed responses reduce transferred bytes. The transport requests gzip compression and decodes it before checking the data. Plain responses also work. A shared gate permits at most 45 request starts per second by default. This is 2,700 starts per minute, below this account’s stated allowance of 3,000 calls per minute. A 429 response pauses all workers and lowers the start rate. Retries are bounded and cancellation stops new requests. One owner saves each completed result. Stock and SPY windows cover up to ten years. Treasury windows remain monthly.

Zero or negative adjusted prices are skipped. Usable prices are saved and the batch continues. Skipped dates remain unavailable. The panel warns you and the exported check report lists those dates. These exclusions stay in the content-bound receipt, so later checks still show them. A completed window does not guarantee a price on each date. A response with only excluded prices is recorded as checked but unavailable. It stores no invented prices and does not stop the batch. Missing or nonfinite values still fail. Malformed rows, duplicate usable dates and dates outside the requested window also fail. The error names the affected file and date window.

Successful requests, including empty responses, are recorded in raw/download-coverage.json. Each entry is tied to the saved file by a content hash. Receipts also retain the original saved span and one previous generation. Interrupted publication can match either exact file generation without losing known unfinished windows. Retry reuses a completed window only while that file remains valid and unchanged. Missing or damaged files lose that completion evidence. They can be downloaded again. Legacy entries without a hash do not prove completion. Actual price dates remain visible. A checked range does not guarantee every session. Short histories can come from IPOs or trading stops. Legacy gaps inside an existing span are not repaired automatically. Managed downloads retain their original saved span and each completed window. A late result cannot hide an unfinished earlier window.

The offline rebuild prepares both databases, compares January holdings, prices and returns with an independent calculation, and rebuilds the website. When the engines agree, changed results can update the reference. Engine disagreement stops publication. Open the strategy page again to load new data. Historical dates remain bounded by the canonical report. Later saved prices can advance latest screening. The separate Full annual financial data download fills missing endpoint assets for the chosen group. It preserves existing valid fields. Each completed endpoint, including an empty response, is bound to its saved content hash. A missing, damaged or changed file must be checked again. Annual statement requests use a 40-report limit; saved coverage is not a promise of complete history.

The panel is served from current source at /data.html. It remains available when essential source files are missing or invalid. In that case startup opens the panel instead of preparing incomplete data. A saved HTML copy needs the local service to inspect or change files.

One project coordinator protects startup, downloads, rebuilds, fixed schedules and random batches across local server instances. Ownership starts before opening a database. It ends after worker completion and database closure. Nested preparation reuses the same ownership. Cancel waits for active requests or the preparation step. Retry waits check for cancellation. A socket wait has a 15-second timeout. Each request uses a 30-second read deadline and at most three attempts. Completed downloads stay saved. Windows can briefly deny a file replacement while another program reads the file. Atomic cache publication retries these access or sharing locks up to eight times. Total retry waits stay below two seconds. Other file errors fail immediately. Cache ownership and receipt-before-asset ordering stay in place. Terminal shutdown waits for the job to release its locks. These data actions accept only same-origin requests from this computer.

The server saves a development log in data/logs/website-<namespace>-<pid>.log. The terminal and data panel show the current file. Each server process has its own log. It keeps job results, provider status, retry counts, affected files and date windows. Error records keep exception types, operating-system codes and stack locations. They omit exception messages, source lines, local variables, API keys, provider URLs and response bodies. Times use UTC. Each process retains one active log and two backups, up to about 5 MiB each. At startup, cleanup removes stopped-process logs older than 14 days. It then removes the oldest stopped-process logs until total log size is at most 100 MiB. Logs from running processes are kept. The filename identifies the process namespace. Windows uses machine identity. Linux uses boot identity and PID namespace. Legacy logs and logs from other namespaces are kept and count toward total size. This includes Linux logs from previous boots. Files with uncertain process ownership or deletion errors are kept. These files can leave total size above the target. Cleanup errors do not stop startup. The limits are checked at startup; logs can grow between starts. The logs stay local and are excluded from Git.

Which download settings were measured?

The 22 October 2026 experiment used native Windows Python 3.12 and uncached dividend-adjusted stock histories. The temporary experiment did not change the active raw cache. For 16 one-year requests, one pooled worker took 22.09–31.81 seconds. Four workers took 5.57–6.84 seconds. Eight took 3.04–3.54 seconds. Sixteen took 4.06 seconds in one round. These transport tests had no steady start-rate cap.

The policy selected on 22 October had eight workers and a four-starts-per-second cap. It saved 16 one-year histories in 6.56 seconds with 16 HTTP 200 responses and no retries. The serial reference took 42.47 seconds. These runs used the same stock symbols but different historical years. They are samples, not a controlled same-period speedup or a universal optimum.

The experiment also found a Python 3.12 response-reuse problem. The transport now closes each exhausted response before the next request. The empty Treasury probe did not establish annual Treasury coverage, so monthly windows remain. Read the 22 October settings and measurements for that evidence.

The 23 October standalone transport experiment made 1,392 distinct stock/window requests. All returned HTTP 200. Across compressed cases, gzip reduced transferred body bytes by 89.1%. Native Windows Python 3.12.1 averaged 207 calls per minute with eight workers and four starts per second. It averaged 1,207 calls per minute with 32 workers and 45 starts per second, without compression. A larger gzip batch on WSL Python 3.14.4 averaged 2,265 calls per minute with 32 workers. The higher worker counts tested were slower.

That experiment supports the current 32-worker, 45-starts-per-second policy with gzip. Its fresh-pool batches lasted about 2–19 seconds. They used different stocks, historical periods and environments. These are prior transport measurements. They are not new application tests, a controlled application speedup, a sustained-rate test or guaranteed throughput. The full data-panel publication path was not measured. Read the 23 October settings and measurements for the scope and limits.

The source now contains the new transport settings. Restart an existing local server to load the current Python code. Reload the data panel to see the current text. Implementation checks use local provider fixtures and temporary caches. They do not download market data.

↻

Replay can be fast because the work is already saved.

In the reference Windows test, 100 fresh trials took 467 seconds. A replay of those saved books took 5.7 seconds. These are different jobs.

What happens to books from the earlier engine?

The startup upgrade keeps saved prices and completed books when the research inputs are unchanged. Version-1 books contain both groups. The upgrade marks both as complete, including empty groups. Version-2 books keep their individual completion markers.

If other source inputs changed, the ordinary offline rebuild is still needed. The completion marker is saved with the group’s records. An interrupted write cannot mark a half-built group as complete.

What happens if I stop a run?

A fixed-date request saves its new books together. A random batch calculates missing books in parallel. It saves all new books for one trial together, in trial order.

Workers only read data. One parent process saves results in SQLite. A failed trial leaves no partial new books. Unfinished writes roll back. Previously saved books remain. Restart the launcher and replay the saved settings and seed. Completed books can be reused. A stopped request does not resume by itself.

06 / Why new trials take time

Plan shared work.
Calculate books in parallel.

The earlier engine prepared both stock groups for every new date pair. The current source prepares only the requested group. Random batches plan unique missing books upfront. Worker processes calculate ahead. One writer saves each complete trial. Each group still gets both supported metrics and holding returns.

Earlier engine / Benchmark reference

New dates→Original groupBroader group→Select stocks

The earlier engine prepared the broader group for an original-group request. New trials created many extra records.

Requested pool and parallel books / In current source

New dates→Requested group only→Parallel books→One writer

Prepare only the group you chose. Plan each missing date pair once. Calculate books with read-only workers. Save complete trials through one SQLite writer. An empty group also counts as complete.

The new Windows comparison took 103.4, 62.0, 40.9 and 33.2 seconds with 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers. A fresh serial requested-group control took 133.3 seconds. Why fewer records help.
The reference test prepared 4,010,439 stock records. The requested-group test prepared 537,906. These are records across periods, not unique companies.

Why shared data is optional.
It added about 12.6 seconds of loading in the 100-trial test. At 24 trials, group-only took 32 seconds. The combined version took 35 seconds.

Can I keep using the current website during development?

The installed website still uses the current slower engine. Editing the WSL source does not replace a running server. The plan requires this website, its backtests, saved results, exports and data panel to remain usable until the replacement is fully ready.

Future experiments and opt-in previews must use isolated resources. A different port or result folder alone is not enough. A benchmark must not hold the live cache lock or stop the user server. User work takes priority. If isolation is not safe, the experiment must wait.

Wave8 adds the first safeguard in WSL source. Normal publication retains the installed commit or resumes the pending publication. Explicit revision changes remain deliberate operator actions. Isolated fixtures verify this selection rule. A live restart and complete benchmark isolation remain unqualified. The current engine stays the default until all financial, speed, interval, workflow, Windows operation and rollback checks pass. A fast pilot alone cannot trigger the switch.

Read the ongoing website availability contract for the required gates. This plan update does not deploy a new engine or change the running website.

How is the next engine's baseline measured?

CB-01 measures the current production engine before replacement work. Its workload file freezes all settings and exact sampled dates. The primary matrix uses 24 annual trials over 1997–2025. It covers both stock groups, three filter profiles and three seeds. The first profile uses the usual top 50. The second adds P/B below 3 and return on equity above 10%. The third requires positive one-year and three-year trailing returns. These are engineering test settings.

Each fresh run uses a disposable database with no saved books. The timed request includes the normal source scan, worker startup, calculation, stock selection and per-trial saving. It also includes response encoding and receipt through a local socket. This adapter uses the website's response events. It does not measure the browser or an HTTP server. Preparation, database copying and large evidence-file writes are excluded.

Saved-book replay is a separate adapter measurement. Timed validation counts saved derived rows. These scans can increase replay time. Do not treat this as production replay latency. Fresh tables are empty. Each case compares all holding fields and aggregate results exactly. The first case also repeats its dates on another fresh database. The harness preserves production books and checks that saved inputs stayed unchanged. Raw-file checks compare paths, sizes and modification times. Database, report and source checks use content hashes. Process memory and I/O are sampled every 200 milliseconds. Sampled peaks can miss brief events. The OS file cache is not cleared.

The CB-01 record holds the frozen workload, completed measurements and pending cases. Full holding evidence stays in the Windows runtime's ignored temporary folder. Earlier measurements above keep their original settings. They are not the new baseline. The harness does not implement a compiled engine or change the website's calculations.

How will optimization methods be compared?

The first CB-02 experiment compared three price engines: sparse Python arrays, compiled NumPy/Numba searches and DuckDB temporal joins. Separate agents built and tested them in parallel. Timed Windows runs used the machine one at a time. They share the current financial policy, filters, ranking and portfolio calculations.

The experimental evaluator loads annual inputs once and saves complete selected trials. It uses temporary in-memory screening tables. These experiments do not change the production pools, prepared databases or website calculations. The original group keeps its 250-candidate pre-price buffer.

Each comparative case has current-engine controls before and after its methods. Current full input scans stay inside headline request times. Loading and compilation are separate costs. A failed or timed-out case remains incomplete. A one-seed pilot cannot qualify a 5× production improvement. The first comparison tests batched price lookup and compact saving. It does not rank complete compiled or SQL financial engines. The first native pilot used the original group, top 50, 24 annual trials over 1997–2025 and seed 42. Arrays took 52.62 seconds and lookup-only Numba took 53.10 seconds. Fresh controls took 78.98 and 115.31 seconds. DuckDB per-book ASOF exceeded its 180-second request budget. No method qualified. Later tests must address the shared report and factor work.

Read the comparative research and the experiment record for measured results, limitations and the next decision.

What does the six-method comparison test?

The third CB-02 experiment tests Numba first, then bulk Python, DuckDB, persistent workers, Polars and Rust. Each method selects eligible annual reports, searches saved prices and calculates numerical factors for several dated books at once. They use the same arithmetic derived from the current financial source. Shared code keeps financial guards, the original buffer order, final SQL selection and portfolio calculations.

These are benchmark prototypes. The website does not use them. The main timing uses the original group, top 50, 24 annual trials over 1997–2025 and seed 42. The current full freshness check stays inside request time. Loading and compilation are separate costs. Fresh production controls bracket each method.

Each method also checks six real books with all threshold fields. Separate correctness requests test financial, trailing-return and mixed filters in both groups. Those requests do not supply performance claims. Completed trials are saved before progress is reported. A native timeout stops the owned process tree and keeps committed evidence. The original comparison runner could continue with other methods after a failure.

All six methods completed the native pilot with exact financial agreement. Numba took 17.55 seconds and Rust took 17.65 seconds. Their times are similar in this single run. The other methods took 21.58–101.81 seconds. The best ratio against the faster adjacent control was 3.34×. No 5× gate passed. The full freshness scan used about 60% of the two fastest requests. These results do not qualify a production engine. Read the six-method record for controls, setup costs, memory and remaining checks.

What does the prepared-validation experiment change?

The fourth CB-02 experiment reduces shared request work in the Numba and Rust benchmarks. These are prototypes. The website and running servers keep the production engine.

Every request still scans the complete annual-file inventory. The scanner compares the same paths, sizes and modification times as the current check. It reads fresh directory entries and avoids repeated metadata calls. Benchmark attachment first compares its inventory with the authoritative scanner. No watcher, time limit or restart-only rule replaces manual-edit detection. A same-size edit with a restored modification time remains outside the existing metadata rule.

A prepared-generation identity also binds the attached numerical inputs, financial policy, source dependencies, prepared metadata and full report content. Unfinished deployment or report publication blocks reuse. A changed generation rejects the request. This benchmark does not repair production data or publish numerical generations.

A request plan preserves every dated book in order. It omits trailing-price searches when no filter needs them. It assembles numerical inputs in batches. Financial guards, formulas, final SQL selection, trial saving and local response delivery stay shared. Validation, calculation, saving, encoding and transport remain inside request time. Attachment and compilation are separate costs.

The native pilot used the original group, top 50, 24 annual trials over 1997–2025 and seed 42. Numba took 12.33 seconds and Rust took 13.41 seconds. Ratios against the faster adjacent production control were 10.49× and 9.58×. All financial comparisons matched exactly. Initial attachment and compilation took about 146 seconds separately for each method. There is no first-use speed claim. The fourth experiment record states control drift, tested recovery and remaining qualification. One original-group seed cannot qualify the full engine or select a production backend.

The fifth measurement wave completed the full matrix on 25 October. It includes both groups, all three filter profiles and all three seeds. Every financial comparison matched exactly. Each case used fresh adjacent controls. Candidate order alternated across seeds. Both methods passed five of six median speed gates. The broader group with trailing return filters failed: Numba 4.66× and Rust 4.53×, below the required 5×. All seed results stay in the record. No production backend is selected. Shared request work needs another experiment before integration. The website keeps the production engine.

The sixth experiment tests one storage change in the Numba benchmark. Each book still calculates both ranking metrics. The temporary SQL tables store only the metric selected for that request. Financial rules, filters, table layout and the SQL selector stay the same. Complete staging provides a contemporary Numba comparison. The declared pilot needs at least a 10% request-time reduction and at least 5× against adjacent production controls before wider tests. These are experiment limits. User workflow budgets remain unresolved. The website keeps the production engine.

The sixth pilot used the broader group, 24 annual trials over 1997–2025 and seed 20261022. Complete staging took 54.17 seconds. Requested-metric staging took 52.04 seconds. The observed reduction was 3.92%, below its declared 10% limit. The production ratio was 4.87×, below 5×. All financial comparisons matched exactly. The intervention stops without wider tests. The next question after that pilot was candidate guards and assembly. Setup took 54.72 and 56.17 seconds separately. These are new pilot measurements, not a full speed gate or a startup result.

The seventh experiment tests candidate guards and record assembly in the Numba benchmark. Both variants keep complete temporary SQL staging. The control runs the source adapters. The treatment compiles decisions derived from the same snapshot, eligibility and metric source. A shared encoder keeps candidate order, dates, status text, missing metric pairs and requested threshold values. Unsupported source structures stop attachment. No handwritten financial guards replace the policy.

Each variant must pass complete-book proofs, ordered holding comparisons and saved-result replay. Failed proof or request evidence now stops the runner before more requests, controls or methods. Cleanup preserves committed trials and closes owned resources. Timing and sampled resource violations also stop the experiment. These changes enforce benchmark evidence rules. They do not change the website engine.

The seventh attempt stopped at its declared 2,700-second whole-experiment limit. All owned processes closed. The source-guard request took 120.20 seconds. Separate setup took 148.33 seconds. Its controls took 691.08 and 598.52 seconds, with 15.46% drift. Source evidence and saved replay matched exactly. The prepared production-input identity matches the sixth wave, but the new controls are slower. The cause is not established.

The compiled candidate never started. The watchdog stopped its first production control. There is no paired request reduction or compiled performance result. Synthetic checks passed in WSL and native Windows, but they do not supply a real-cache speed gate. Expansion is rejected. The next bounded design must account for observed measurement and control costs. Financial rules, immediate freshness and the full six-case speed gate stay required. Production databases, source and report stayed unchanged.

The master plan was revised on 25 October. Numba remains the working direction. The guard and assembly prototype needs a complete bounded pair before wider qualification. The full six-case 5× gate still blocks production integration. Rust remains available if a concrete Numba limitation requires another comparison. Immediate manual-edit detection stays required under the existing path, size and modification-time rule.

The plan separates faster existing month workflows from the weekly extension. Weekly support remains required before program completion and default cutover. Startup, fresh research, changed filters and saved-result reopening need agreed time budgets. Those budgets are not set yet. A separate complete trailing-filter test will supplement the original test, whose trials contain an empty period. The original failed test stays in the speed gate.

Implementation findings can change the master plan. Each change must record its evidence, affected work and remaining decisions. Earlier measurements stay in their original records. Changes to acceptance criteria or financial rules require a user decision. These are planning decisions. They do not change a running server.

How is the live website kept available during development?

The stable website must stay usable until the replacement passes every readiness gate. The wave8 prerequisite changes normal publication to retain the installed revision. It does not change the current server, its dependencies or its saved data.

Wave9 adds a closed admission policy to the WSL benchmark tools. Executable runs and timed request adapters reject before financial access. Source-only imports and numerical fixture helpers remain available. No flag, environment variable or temporary folder can admit a run. This safeguard does not change installed tools or the running server.

Benchmark isolation is still unproved. A later input owner must bind the same consistent generation to both engines. It must separate candidate source, dependencies, compiler caches, mutable databases and result stores from the stable service. CPU, memory, disk and cancellation limits also need proofs. A separate result folder or port is insufficient. Do not repeat the seventh wave’s live-cache-locking pair. The wave9 prerequisite implements no input capture. No real-cache pilot follows from either safeguard.

The wave10 prerequisite adds a synthetic input store on a separate development branch and WSL worktree. A producer constructs private research and daily databases with a bound report. It closes writers before it publishes an immutable generation. Readers use read-only connections. Each writable daily clone belongs to a separate experiment directory.

This store does not copy the live databases. The current exclusive cache lock can make user work wait during a copy. A rollback-journal reader can also delay writer commits. Copies made while the website runs need a qualified immutable handoff producer and resource checks first. Synthetic size, memory and deadline checks are cooperative. They do not qualify live capture or admit a benchmark. The normal launcher still uses the original registered checkout.

The wave11 offline copy tool can capture databases after the user stops the server. It takes exclusive source ownership, then financial ownership. An active owner rejects the copy. A server start can wait until the copy ends. The tool uses SQLite backup and preserves saved books and report bytes. It rejects unfinished publication and unsupported journal states. It checks originals again before it publishes the separate copy. This does not admit a benchmark or qualify copying while the website runs.

The wave12 input workspace checks the copied databases, report and actual source files as one captured generation. It keeps captured databases read-only. Each writable derivative belongs to its own experiment workspace. All database handles close before workspace ownership ends. The saved inventory describes capture time. It cannot replace a current raw-file check. This bounded tool does not attach financial engines or admit a real-data run. The next engine adapter must bind both engines and policy without hidden paths to the original databases.

The wave13 policy attachment constructs the actual financial policy in one owned source-only child process. It imports verified private source. This keeps import effects out of the parent process. The parent receives an immutable binding of policy, source and captured financial generation. The child closes before workspace ownership ends. If cleanup cannot be confirmed, experiment ownership stays held for retry. It has no financial request command. Current raw freshness, numerical inputs and reference controls still need a qualified engine facade. Source-only child checks do not qualify general execution resources or admit a real-data run.

The measured-execution work brings reference controls and both Numba guard variants under one owner. It uses actual private financial source and disposable databases. It compares complete books, holdings, summaries and saved replay. The owner keeps private files and child processes until cleanup is confirmed. A failed cleanup keeps ownership for retry. Current file checks are inside each fixture request.

This is a disposable fixture capability. Real benchmark admission stays closed. New source announces live work before it waits for cache ownership. A coordinated observation takes shared source ownership first. It then takes short cache ownership. It checks for live intent between work units and gives up when live work arrives. It closes its database handles before it releases ownership. Calculation holds no live coordinator. Live intent during calculation stops only the experiment.

This is cooperative priority. An operation can wait until the current observation unit and cleanup finish. It is not a zero-delay guarantee. The provider checks actual participating source. A marker cannot enable it. The installed older runtime does not gain this contract from a source edit. No installed source or server changed.

Native fixture jobs now limit committed memory, process count and CPU share before work starts. Committed memory is different from resident memory. Frames, total transport bytes and queued events have bounds. The owner registers before child creation. Failed startup keeps ownership until cleanup is confirmed. Cleanup checks leader exit, output end, reader closure and job emptiness separately. Linux sessions cannot prevent every descendant from leaving. Resident-memory, thread and disk enforcement remain incomplete. These gaps keep the full resource gate open. Real runs still need production-scale resource and website availability checks. The earlier input workspace keeps its original small limits.

The next resource checkpoint adds an outside supervisor. The complete application controller runs inside an owned resource domain. It still uses the same reference and Numba calculations. Native Windows uses the existing Job Object. WSL uses a private transient user service. Its kernel controls bound charged memory, combined process and thread counts, and CPU allocation. A child that changes its process session stays in that service. Direct fixture contexts keep their earlier scope.

Charged memory is different from total mapped residency. The outside supervisor is outside the application limits. The optional lifetime boundary described below contains supervision and collection under a separate ancestor. Aggregate disk use, total CPU time, native thread enforcement and blocked kernel calls remain unqualified. Optional WSL storage now uses a private temporary filesystem through evidence collection. Native aggregate storage and the complete resource envelope remain unqualified. These gaps keep real admission closed.

The supervisor can cancel a blocked controller without waiting for an application checkpoint. It accepts a result only after domain closure and terminal receipt publication. A failed close keeps its owner and control files for retry. A dead creation client and an absent service cannot settle an unknown creation request. Ownership stays held until creation or manager teardown is confirmed. A successful controller result write also consumes the finalization budget. Launch and import count toward attachment. Domain closure and receipt publication count toward finalization and whole time. A generated 36,160-file inventory test extends cooperative handoff checks. It does not qualify production financial size, HTTP, browser use, restart or installed source.

The synthetic HTTP checkpoint now exercises actual copied handlers on a private loopback service. Its generated data has 16 companies and 20,880 price rows. It checks five random trials, cached reuse, saved-date inspection and complete response delivery. An arriving HTTP request makes an observation yield. A separate experimental calculation also stops for live work. Only the experiment stops.

A disconnected stream keeps its completed trial. A fresh service interpreter reuses those saved books. The disposable service keeps source ownership until its listener and request threads close. These checks use private prepared-storage bindings. They do not qualify production preparation, service freshness, browser controls, CSV downloads, real-data capacity, the normal launcher or installed restart. The main-page fixture checks static delivery. The data panel uses copied source. Full resources and real admission remain unqualified.

The native user CPU checkpoint gives the supervised Windows application one cumulative user-time threshold. The job settings are checked before bootstrap. Startup, nested workers, detached children, native library threads and exited processes share that threshold. Ordinary workers do not receive a new copy of the budget. Final accounting stays available after job closure. Exhaustion rejects a queued successful result.

Windows checks this threshold periodically. Small fixtures show substantial overshoot before termination. It is not an exact CPU ceiling. The application threshold excludes kernel CPU and supervision outside its job. The separate ancestor described below has its own native user-time threshold. WSL cumulative CPU enforcement remains unsupported. The complete resource and availability gates stay open. These settings are disposable test limits. They are not user workflow budgets or real admission.

The storage checkpoint adds an optional WSL storage boundary inside the same supervisor. One private tmpfs holds writable source copies, databases, journals, compiler caches, temporary files and results. Shared memory uses the same allowance. Original inputs and host paths stay read-only. Observation uses existing lock files through read-only handles. It keeps the same source-before-cache order and live priority.

A transferred directory handle keeps storage available after every application process closes. The supervisor then collects evidence into one fixed-size persistent container. Complete checksummed records survive an interrupted copy. Failed collection or closure keeps ownership for retry. A failed comparison stays failed. If the last supervisor dies, uncollected tmpfs bytes can be lost. A ready container never proves accepted return.

The financial fixture declares 32 MiB of tmpfs capacity, 40 MiB for persistent evidence and 1 MiB for control-file payloads. The tmpfs limit covers allocated data blocks. Sparse file lengths, inode counts, filesystem metadata, total memory and I/O are different. The persistent writer has a finite allowance. It is not a disk quota. Collection and publication stay inside finalization time. Native aggregate storage remains unsupported after its private probe. Full resources and real admission stay open.

The supervisor lifetime checkpoint adds an optional WSL ancestor boundary. A private transient slice contains the supervisor helper and application service. Its memory, swap, combined task and CPU allocation settings are checked before work starts. The supervisor, its manager clients, readers, pinned storage and evidence collection share that ancestor. The application keeps its own inner limits.

Application closure does not release this boundary. Retained temporary-file pages remain charged beneath the ancestor during collection. A manager deadline closes the helper after caller death. The application is bound to that helper. Unknown creation or closure keeps ownership for explicit retry. An alive helper can retry mechanical cleanup. A killed helper loses its Python objects. Completed container records remain verifiable. Uncollected temporary-file bytes can be lost.

The lifetime financial fixture uses 2,304 MiB of charged memory, 96 combined tasks and 25% CPU allocation. It keeps the earlier 32 MiB temporary filesystem and 40 MiB evidence container. Two request files and bounded action files add a separate 2 MiB plus 8 KiB control allowance. These are fixture limits. The invoking caller and its helper-launch client and reader remain outside the ancestor. Initial manager submission and final ownership calls also remain outside. Total residency, cumulative CPU, hard I/O and global archive retention remain open. The WSL declaration keeps its charged-memory and task meanings. A separate Windows declaration uses the native controls described below. Native aggregate storage remains unsupported. Omitted declarations keep the earlier weaker scope. Real admission stays closed.

The native lifetime checkpoint extends the same helper boundary to Windows. Its explicit Windows declaration sets aggregate committed memory, active processes, CPU allocation and periodic user CPU termination. The suspended root cannot run before these settings and handle ownership are checked. Its application uses a nested job. Application exit does not release the outer job. Final accounting includes exited descendants and helper finalization.

The native financial fixture declares 2,304 MiB of committed memory, 16 active processes, 25% CPU allocation and 180 user CPU seconds. The application keeps its separate 2 GiB, eight-process and 120-user-second settings. Nested CPU caps can further restrict work. These are fixture limits. They do not set user time budgets or prove real performance.

The caller keeps the outer job handle. It is not inheritable. Caller death closes that handle and terminates the owned processes. Closure checks process exit, output end, reader closure, job emptiness, final accounting and handle release. A live helper can retry failed cleanup. A killed helper leaves only the evidence already written. A complete message cannot override final CPU exhaustion. The original finalization clock runs through outer closure.

Windows committed memory is different from total resident memory. Process limits do not bound threads. User CPU checks are periodic and can overshoot. Total CPU, strict CPU ceilings, native aggregate storage and hard I/O remain open. The caller and its reader remain outside the job. Native evidence uses private ordinary files. It supplies no disk quota. Real admission and full resource qualification stay closed.

The revised plan keeps tested Numba calculations. The additional compiled guards from wave7 remain a separate real-data question. It reuses demonstrated calculations, SQL selection, portfolio aggregation and saved-trial evidence. Later work strengthens those contracts. It does not rebuild each layer merely to follow the old phase order.

A new comparison uses one current-engine control before both Numba variants and another after them. Its protocol declares costs for attachment, copies, setup, proofs, requests, evidence and cleanup. An interrupted run cannot finish a later timing pair. The source-only prospective declaration allocates 6,960 seconds within a 7,200-second whole bound. Each step has separate limits. Controls must stay within a 1.20 ratio and one 6,600-second bracket. These are experiment stop limits. They are not predictions or user time budgets. Its real binding and qualification remain pending. Validating its arithmetic cannot admit a run. Read the hardening record for scope and checks. These fixture checks give no new speed result. The user changed the six-case minimum to 4× on 26 October 2026. The 10× target, immediate edit detection and weekly scope stay required. Historical reports retain their original criteria and verdicts. This acceptance change supplies no new timing or qualification. User workflow budgets remain unresolved. The stable engine and compatible old evidence remain available through qualification and tested rollback.

What does the complete fictional website check prove?

The benchmark-only source-service check starts with 64 fictional companies. Its weekday calendar runs from 1992 to 21 October 2026. Current copied source prepares the January and daily databases. The independent engine must agree on all 31 baseline books and their 50 holdings. The ordinary builder creates the page and exports. It does not use prepared-table substitutes or a placeholder page.

The check uses the real latest, historical, fixed-date and random-date controls. Browser downloads must match SQL or ordinary HTTP results. It checks saved-date inspection, reload and replay, empty selections, data inspection and rebuild. A saved-input edit must reject stale requests. A latest-only price update must keep historical results. A private missing-key path keeps the real key untouched. No market-data download runs.

The service owns copied source before application imports. It releases source after data jobs, request threads and its listener close. Page and panel delivery remain available during a saved-data rebuild. Financial requests wait for ordinary cache ownership to end. Cooperative observation yields to arriving work. These are separate behaviors; this does not prove zero-delay access.

This fixture has separate storage and service allowances. Size checks are not disk quotas. Its cold databases exceed the older 32 MiB capture fixture allowance. That older allowance does not change. That earlier source-service check did not qualify combined attachment. The later combined-service check qualifies its separately declared fictional workload. The Linux browser checks the WSL service. Native HTTP checks pass. That check used a Linux browser. A later private native-browser check also passes on the same fictional source fixture. It compares six scenario groups and seven saved CSV files with SQL and ordinary function results. Read the native-browser record for this separate evidence. The check does not qualify real-data capacity, installed compatibility, browser resources or full isolation. Real admission stays closed. Read the source-service record for its exact evidence and limits.

Can the complete fictional generation run beside its source service?

A separate benchmark check joins the full fictional generation to the existing measurement owner. Ordinary source prepares the data. The fictional service closes. The existing offline capture owner copies and verifies the database/report pair. The service then restarts unchanged. Both controls and both Numba variants use the same immutable capture.

The new synthetic declaration allows 64 MiB of input databases and 256 MiB of private output. It does not change the older public capture fixture's 32 MiB input limit. That older fixture still rejects this larger generation. WSL strict storage has a separate 256 MiB writable limit and a 272 MiB evidence container. Native aggregate storage remains unsupported. These fixture settings do not admit a real run or set user budgets.

Each timed request still checks the current source service files, metadata, report and journals. Observation closes before private calculation. A live financial request must acquire ownership within two seconds and stop only the experiment. Page and panel delivery, cancellation, saved-book inspection and restart use actual handlers. An interrupted bracket cannot become an accepted pair.

One fictional workspace retains the registered service, comparison and output owners. Cleanup closes them before deleting inputs. Unknown closure keeps both roots for explicit retry. A retry cannot erase the original failure. Read the combined-service record for its exact qualification. Real resources, installed compatibility and real performance remain open. Native browser interaction has separate fictional-fixture evidence.

What does the private native-browser check prove?

An existing Windows Chrome browser uses a new private profile. A test-only owner starts it inside the existing Windows Job before application work begins. It connects only to the debugger address recorded by that profile. It does not attach to an existing browser or use the installed website.

The check uses real pointer clicks and ordinary control events. It saves each CSV through the browser. Download events, file bytes and hashes establish each completed download. Latest, historical, fixed-date and random-date results agree with the fictional fixture’s SQL and ordinary function evidence. The mobile main page and data panel have no horizontal overflow. Check and Rebuild use saved fictional inputs.

Browser shutdown confirms that descendants, streams and Job handles close before either private root is removed. Unknown closure retains owners for retry. Logical storage checks are not disk quotas. Job commit, process, CPU-share and periodic user-time limits do not prove total residency, hard thread limits, hard I/O or complete isolation. This check gives no new performance result and opens no real admission.

What does the report-index experiment change?

The second CB-02 experiment indexes saved annual-report dates. It preserves report availability, report age and the original buffer order. It uses the same array price engine and financial calculations. With no threshold conditions, it skips unused threshold calculations and trailing-price lookups. With any condition, it calls the complete current threshold calculator. It still calculates both ranking metrics.

The full freshness check stays inside request time. Setup and saved-result replay are separate from a fresh request. Failed runs retain setup, memory and completed-trial evidence. This evaluator is a benchmark prototype. The website does not use it.

Its native pilot used the original group, top 50, 24 annual trials over 1997–2025 and seed 42. All financial results matched exactly. The warm request took 58.13 seconds. Fresh controls took 99.72 and 179.84 seconds. The ratio against the faster control was 1.72×. Control drift was 80%, so this is a descriptive pilot result. The freshness check used 44.10 seconds. Source and price attachment added 90.56 seconds outside the request. No 5× gate passed. The other 17 primary cases remain unmeasured for this method. Read the second experiment record for evidence and the next decision.

Source code and a running server can differ.

The requested-pool change is now in the source. Upfront planning and parallel book calculation are also applied. Four workers are the automatic default for batches with at least 64 missing books. Small batches stay serial. Shared in-memory data remains a prototype. Normal backtest-web.cmd starts retain the installed revision. Use an explicit WSL revision command only when a deliberate source update is authorized.

Where is the Git history in this workspace?

The repository history is in .git-local/. The normal .git/ folder is empty and read-only. Git apps may not detect the repository automatically.

From the project folder, run git --git-dir=.git-local --work-tree=. status. Use the same options for log, diff, add and commit. If the default Git wrapper fails with a WSL socket error, use /usr/bin/git with these options. Keep the existing history.

Which report is the current reference?

Use results/summary-exits.txt. It keeps a stock at its last price when trading stops.

New saved prices can change a past result, even when the Through date stays the same. Preparation runs the SQL engine and the independent reference engine on the same saved files and historical cutoff. Both must agree on every year, selected stock, rank, fiscal report, price date, price, valuation, exit basis and return. Numbers use a tight floating-point tolerance. Equal annual averages cannot hide a holding mismatch.

Prepare both results→Compare priced holdings→Keep revision evidence→Publish report + database

Agreement permits a changed reference. Engine disagreement stops publication and keeps the previous outputs. The Through date stays fixed. Later SPY sessions can advance latest screening independently.

Revision folders in results/baseline-history/ retain the previous report verbatim, previous and new priced holdings, and an audit of changed years, stocks, prices and returns. The data panel shows the last revision after a check or rebuild. Use Export baseline revision to save its JSON evidence. The first verification cannot recover old prices that were never stored. It labels those prices as unavailable.

A journal records an unfinished report/database replacement. Readers reject that unfinished generation. Retry preparation to complete its hash-verified publication. Relative evidence paths and logical targets permit recovery after moving the folder or switching between Windows and WSL. Keep the journal and its referenced files. Schema 6 stores the priced observations and report identity in the research database. Unchanged inputs skip both calculations. A latest-only update keeps the last historical revision.

scripts/run.py still uses the older exit rule and writes to results/legacy/. Those files are not the current reference.

How does the website adapt to a phone?

Desktop filters use four columns. Tablet filters use two columns. Phone filters use one column. Phone summary cards stack vertically. Buttons and form controls have a minimum height of 44 pixels.

Wide charts and tables scroll inside their panels. Scroll instructions remain visible. Stock symbols stay visible as stock tables scroll sideways. Tap a chart mark to read its detail below the chart. Mouse and keyboard interaction also work.

These layouts apply to latest picks, January books, custom schedules and random trials. The built HTML includes the styles and interactions. Rebuild the website after a source change. A page already open in a browser needs a reload.

What do the charts and downloads show?

Browser downloads reflect the current selection. Baseline export files remain separate. Historical views show period returns and the growth of an equal-weight portfolio.

A stock’s contribution is its holding return divided by the actual stock count. Gain and loss pies are scaled separately. Their slices are not shares of net return.

The return distribution chart shows trial counts for the current seed. CAGR and total return show strategy and paired SPY on the same bins and axes. You can also select the CAGR difference from SPY. Each series has its own mean marker. A dashed bell curve fits each series with nonzero standard deviation. This fit does not show that returns follow a normal distribution. Incomplete trials are excluded. Identical returns show one bar without a fitted curve.

The average random-trial CAGR is an average of trial results. It is not one portfolio return. Trial percentiles are not confidence intervals.

Which limits should I keep in mind?
  • The strategy uses equal starting weights and no commissions.
  • The saved-price group does not cover the full market.
  • Sector, exchange and listing status come from saved company metadata.
  • The 90-day report delay is an assumption. It is not a verified filing date.
  • Some supplier figures can include later revisions.
  • New early stops outside the original review can need further checks.

08 / Words used in this guide

The terms, without the code.

Cache
Saved data that the program can use again.
Book
The stock records for one buy date and one sell or mark date.
Pool / Stock group
The set of candidate stocks used for selection. It is separate from the final stock count.
Snapshot
A saved stock record for a particular date or holding period.
Filter
A condition that a stock must meet before ranking.
Rank
A stock’s position after filtering and sorting by the selected metric.
Rebalance
Select stocks again and give each selected stock the same starting weight.
Trial
One complete backtest with one set of sampled trade dates.
Seed / Date-set number
A number used to repeat random date choices with the same saved data and settings.
SQLite
A database engine that reads and writes local files. It does not need a separate database server.
Market cap
The estimated market value of the company’s equity.
EV / Enterprise value
In this model, estimated market cap plus report net debt.
EBITDA
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. The model derives it from saved annual metrics.
EBITDA/EV and EV/EBITDA
Reciprocal ratios. A higher positive EBITDA/EV means a lower positive EV/EBITDA.
P/B
Price divided by book value. This filter needs saved annual equity and a rebuild.
CAGR
The constant annual growth rate that would produce the same total growth over the test window.
SPY
The S&P 500 ETF used for comparison. Its saved return series includes dividends.
API / Local service
The browser’s way to ask Python for a dated calculation. These requests use saved data on your computer.
